nameStory: The squarestem spikerush gets its name from its most distinctive feature - a stem that's sharply four-angled rather than round like most plants. When you roll it between your fingers, you'll feel those four distinct edges that make it 'square' in cross-section. The 'spikerush' part comes from its spike-like flower cluster that sits atop the stem like a tiny brown club.
description: Squarestem spikerush is a wetland grass-like plant that looks deceptively simple at first glance. It grows in clumps of slender, leafless stems that reach about 1-3 feet tall, each topped with a single brown, oval flower spike. Despite its grass-like appearance, it's actually a sedge - part of a plant family known for their often triangular or angular stems. This particular species stands out because of its uniquely four-sided stems that feel spongy when you squeeze them.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: The stem is sharply four-angled - roll it between your fingers and you'll feel four distinct ridges. The stem is also spongy and compressible, like squeezing a small foam tube.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Single brown spike sits at the tip of each stem, looking like a small oval club about 1-3 inches long. The spike is made up of light brown, papery scales (bracts) that overlap like shingles.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows in colonies from underground rhizomes (spreading roots), creating patches of seemingly leafless stems. Each stem is unbranched and stands straight up from the water or muddy ground.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Has no obvious leaves - just small, brownish sheaths that wrap around the base of the stem near ground level. The green stem does all the photosynthesis work.

idTips.label: Habitat Context
idTips.description: Always found with its 'feet wet' - growing directly in shallow water or on muddy shores that flood regularly. Never found in dry upland areas.

habitat: Look for squarestem spikerush along the edges of ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams where it can keep its roots constantly wet. It thrives in the shallow water zone and muddy shores that flood and recede with water levels. You'll often find it mixed with other wetland sedges, cattails, and rushes in these marshy areas.

seasonality.spring: New green stems emerge from underwater rhizomes as water warms. Young stems are especially spongy to the touch and bright green.
seasonality.summer: Peak identification time when brown flower spikes are most prominent atop mature stems. The four-angled stems are fully developed and easy to feel.
seasonality.fall: Flower spikes turn darker brown and may persist. Seeds ripen and disperse. Stems begin to yellow but the square shape remains obvious.
seasonality.winter: Most above-ground growth dies back, but some dried stems may persist through winter, still showing the characteristic square cross-section when examined.

funFact: The spongy, four-angled stems act like tiny snorkels, with air-filled chambers that transport oxygen down to the roots living in oxygen-poor mud underwater - it's basically wearing its own built-in scuba gear!
confusionNotes: Most other spikerushes have round stems, so the square stem is your best clue. If you're not sure, do the 'finger roll test' - roll the stem between your thumb and finger, and you should feel four distinct edges rather than a smooth round surface.
contextualKnowledge: Despite looking like a grass, squarestem spikerush is actually a sedge. Remember the old botanist saying: 'sedges have edges' - and this one really drives the point home with its dramatically four-sided stems. It's one of the easier sedges to identify because of this unique feature.
compareHints: Among the many spikerush species in New England, squarestem spikerush is the only one with distinctly four-angled stems - all the others have round or slightly flattened stems. Common spikerush and needle spikerush, the two you're most likely to encounter, both have completely round, smooth stems. The square stem makes this species unmistakable once you know what to feel for.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the many spikerush species in New England, blunt spikerush stands out for its soft, spongy stems and distinctly rounded spikelets.
Needle Spikerush is the most delicate of all New England spikerushes, with stems so thin they make other species look chunky by comparison.
Unlike other spikerushes that grow in shallow water or wet soil, Robbins' Spikerush is the deep-water specialist of the genus, growing fully submerged in 1-4 feet of water.

Among the many spikerush species in New England, Black-fruited Spikerush is most easily distinguished by its dark seeds - Common Spikerush has pale tan seeds, while Needle Spikerush is much more delicate with thread-like stems.
Among the many New England spikerushes, Yellow Spikerush stands out for its pale, yellowish coloring and smaller stature compared to Common Spikerush or Blunt Spikerush.
Among New England spikerushes, common spikerush is distinguished by its robust, colony-forming habit and relatively large flower spikes.
Among New England's many spikerush species, Small Spikerush is distinguished by its extremely short stature (under 4 inches) and preference for salty habitats.
Among New England's many spikerushes, Matted Spikerush is unique for its low, mat-forming growth habit - all its relatives grow upright.
Among its many spikerush relatives in New England, ovate spikerush stands out with its distinctly oval or egg-shaped flower spikes - most other spikerushes have more cylindrical or pointed spikes.
Among New England's many spikerushes, Slender Spikerush stands out for its particularly thin stems and small, oval flower spikes.
Among New England's spikerushes, Wright's is distinguished by its small size and the distinctive pyramid-shaped tubercle on its seeds.
Among the many New England spikerushes, Horsetail Spikerush is unique for its hollow, jointed stems - most other spikerushes have solid stems without visible segments.

Few-flower Spikerush stands out from its many spikerush relatives primarily by its sparse flower count - most other New England spikerushes like Common Spikerush or Blunt Spikerush have dense, crowded spikelets with dozens of flowers.
Among New England's many spikerushes, Long-tubercled Spikerush stands out for its exceptionally large tubercle - up to 2.
Beaked spikerush differs from its many spikerush relatives primarily in its habitat preferences and the distinctive beaked tubercle on its seeds.
Among New England's spikerushes, Slender Spikerush has the thinnest stems - much thinner than Common Spikerush or Blunt Spikerush.

Among the spikerushes, Bald Spikerush stands out for its particularly wide, oval flower spikes with a reddish tint, unlike the narrow spikes of Needle Spikerush or the larger, brown spikes of Common Spikerush.

Unlike Common Spikerush which has smooth, round stems, or Needle Spikerush which forms dense mats of hair-thin stems, Threerib Spikerush is the only species in the genus with distinctly three-ribbed stems.
Among New England's many spikerushes, Creeping Spikerush is unique for its mat-forming, spreading growth pattern via underground runners.
